overview: Bolivia is a landlocked country in the heart of South America. Its seat of government is La Paz, while Sucre is the constitutional capital. Bolivia won independence from Spain in 1825 and is named after the independence leader Simón Bolívar. Many Bolivians are of Indigenous descent, and its constitution recognises Spanish and more than 30 Indigenous languages as official.

geography.text: Western Bolivia is high: the Andes surround the Altiplano, a high plateau where La Paz stands and where Lake Titicaca lies on the border with Peru. The Salar de Uyuni on the Altiplano is the largest salt flat in the world. The east of the country is much lower, with tropical rainforest and grasslands in the Amazon basin.

subsections.title: Climate
subsections.text: Cold and dry on the high Altiplano, hot and wet in the Amazon lowlands.

subsections.title: Wildlife
subsections.text: Llamas, alpacas and vicuñas in the Andes; flamingos on salt lakes; jaguars and river dolphins in the Amazon.

history.text: The Bolivian Andes were home to the Tiwanaku civilisation and later became part of the Inca Empire. Under Spanish rule the silver mines of Potosí made it one of the richest places on Earth. Bolivia won independence in 1825 but later lost its coastline to Chile in the War of the Pacific. In 2006 Evo Morales became its first Indigenous president.

events.title: Potosí silver
events.text: Huge silver deposits are found at Potosí.

events.title: Independence
events.text: Bolivia becomes independent and is named after Simón Bolívar.

events.title: War of the Pacific
events.text: Bolivia loses its coast to Chile.

events.title: Chaco War
events.text: A war with Paraguay over the Chaco region.

government.text: Bolivia is a presidential republic; its constitution calls it a 'plurinational state', recognising its many Indigenous nations. The President is elected every five years. La Paz is the seat of government, while Sucre is the constitutional capital. It recognises 37 official languages.

economy.text: Bolivia's economy relies on natural gas, mining, especially zinc, silver and tin, and farming. Its salt flats hold some of the world's largest lithium reserves, used in batteries. Many people work in informal jobs.

culture.text: More than half of Bolivians are Indigenous, mainly Quechua and Aymara. The Carnival of Oruro, with its Diablada devil dance, is listed by UNESCO. Women in La Paz often wear bowler hats and layered skirts, and some compete as 'cholita' wrestlers.

items.title: Salar de Uyuni
items.text: The world's largest salt flat, which turns into a giant mirror after rain.

items.title: Carnival of Oruro
items.text: A festival of masked dances listed by UNESCO.

items.title: Mi Teleférico
items.text: La Paz's cable cars, the highest urban cable car network in the world.

subsections.title: Food
subsections.text: Salteñas, juicy baked pastries filled with meat stew, are eaten in the morning.

subsections.title: Music and arts
subsections.text: Andean music with pan pipes and the charango, a small guitar.

subsections.title: Traditions and festivals
subsections.text: The Carnival of Oruro, with devil dancers in huge masks, is listed by UNESCO.

sport.text: Football is the most popular sport. Bolivia's capital La Paz sits at about 3,600 metres, and visiting teams often struggle with the thin air. Bolivia won the South American Championship in 1963.

items.text: Bolivia won the Copa América as host.

items.title: Estadio Hernando Siles
items.text: One of the highest international football stadiums in the world.

didYouKnow: La Paz is the highest seat of government in the world, at about 3,600 metres.
Bolivia has a navy, even though it has no coastline; it patrols Lake Titicaca and rivers.

keyPeople.name: Evo Morales
keyPeople.text: Bolivia's first Indigenous president, from 2006 to 2019.
